title: Glossary and decision guide
summary: A glossary of the trail's key terms, decision tables from requirements to choices, the ten reference architectures compared, and an interview checklist.

blocks.text: Each term points to the chapter where it is explained in depth. Definitions are deliberately short; they are recall aids, not substitutes.

blocks.text: In interviews, define a term and then name the trade-off it implies. *Merge-on-read* is cheap writes and slower reads until compaction; saying the second half is what shows experience.
Start from requirements, not tools. Each table maps a requirement signal to a default choice; defaults are where you start, and the ADR records why you deviated.

blocks.title: Applying the guide
blocks.text: A team needs 10-minute freshness, uses Spark and Snowflake, and has two data engineers.
items: Latency: micro-batch, not streaming.
Storage: Iceberg lakehouse, Snowflake reading through a catalog (chapter 47).
Catalog: REST or the cloud catalog; one writer engine.
Modelling: star in gold; orchestration: Dagster or Airflow; metrics in a headless semantic layer.

blocks.text: 50.4 The ten reference architectures side by side
Real platforms mix these. Chapters 47-49 each combine three or four of them; the table is for naming the parts, not for choosing a single box.

items: Draw an end-to-end architecture for a stated freshness target and justify each hop.
Explain log-based CDC, replication slots and how deletes propagate (chapter 17).
Explain event time, watermarks and late data with one concrete example (chapter 6).
Walk through an Iceberg commit: data files, manifests, manifest list, metadata file, catalog swap (chapter 22).
Compare copy-on-write and merge-on-read and name the maintenance each needs (chapters 23, 25).
Design a star schema from a business process: grain first, then dimensions and facts (chapter 8).
Explain SCD2 and how to build it incrementally (chapter 9).
Describe how Snowflake reads Iceberg and which engine writes (chapter 28).
Show a MERGE that is idempotent under replays.
Name three data quality checks and where they run (chapter 33).
Explain masking, row access policies and GDPR erasure across snapshots (chapters 34, 49).
Define a ratio metric correctly in a semantic layer (chapter 35).
Estimate volumes: events per second, bytes per event, daily and yearly storage.

blocks.title: Your own decision record
blocks.text: Pick a system you know (from work or a case in chapters 47-49) and write a one-page ADR using the decision tables above: requirements with numbers, three options from the reference architectures, the chosen design, consequences and a revisit condition.
hints: Which requirement actually drives the design, and which ones are nice-to-have?
What would have to change for your second-best option to win?

items: Every term in the glossary implies a trade-off; learn both halves.
Choose latency model, storage, catalog, modelling, orchestration and semantic layer from requirements.
Defaults are a starting point; an ADR records deviations and when to revisit them.
The ten reference architectures are building blocks that real platforms combine.
Interview answers are strongest with numbers, failure modes and operations, not only boxes.

blocks.q: A team needs dashboards updated within seconds but no per-event business logic. What does the guide suggest?
options: Hourly batch with a faster warehouse
Lambda architecture with a batch and speed layer
Streaming ingest into a real-time OLAP store
blocks.explain: Fresh aggregates for dashboards are what real-time OLAP stores do; stream jobs are for stateful per-event logic, and Lambda doubles the pipelines.

blocks.q: Which situation most favours an Iceberg lakehouse over a single cloud warehouse?
options: One SQL team and strong central governance
Spark, ML and Snowflake must work on one copy of the data
Small data volumes and a single BI tool
blocks.explain: Multi-engine access to one open copy is the core lakehouse benefit; the other options favour a warehouse.

options: That no events older than time T are still expected
That processing time equals event time
That all events have been written to Iceberg
blocks.explain: A watermark is a completeness assertion about event time; late events are those arriving after it passes.

blocks.q: Why does the decision guide pair defaults with an ADR?
options: Deviations need a recorded reason and a condition for revisiting
ADRs are required by Iceberg catalogs
blocks.explain: Defaults fit common cases; the ADR captures context so later teams know why and when to change.
